title: WHY JOSHUA MADE THEM CARRY 12 HEAVY STONES OUT OF THE JORDAN
paragraphs: WHY JOSHUA MADE THEM CARRY 12 HEAVY STONES OUT OF THE JORDAN

They had already crossed the river. They were already safe. God had already performed the miracle. So why did Joshua send twelve men back into the place they had just escaped… and tell each one to put a heavy stone on his shoulder? Because God knew something about the human heart Israel was about to discover: sometimes surviving the miracle is easier than remembering the God who performed it.
The river was behind them.
Imagine the scene.
Children who had grown up hearing stories about the Red Sea were suddenly standing on the other side of their own impossible water.
Parents were gathering their families.
Feet that had walked through the Jordan were finally touching the soil of Canaan.
For forty years, Israel had wandered.
Forty years of funerals.
Forty years of dust.
Forty years of consequences.
Forty years of hearing about a land that always seemed to exist somewhere beyond tomorrow.
And now…
they were standing in it.
But before Israel could rush toward Jericho, before the walls fell, before battles were fought and territories were possessed, God gave Joshua a strange command.
Go back to the river.
Choose twelve men.
One from every tribe.
And tell each man to pick up a stone.
Not a pebble.
Not a souvenir small enough to slip unnoticed into his pocket.
Joshua 4:5 says:
“Take you up every man of you a stone upon his shoulder…”
Upon his shoulder.
Something with weight.
Something he would feel while carrying it.
Something that would make forgetting inconvenient.
The Hebrew word translated “stone” is אֶבֶן — ʾeven.
And the command appears in a story saturated with another Hebrew idea:
זָכַר — zākar.
To remember.
Not merely to recall information.
Biblical remembrance is often active. It brings the past into the present so that what God has done shapes how His people live now.
And God knew Israel would need that.
Because the greatest danger after a miracle is sometimes not another river.
It is forgetting who brought you through the first one.
That may be where this story stops being ancient history and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because you have crossed some Jordans too.
There were nights you thought would destroy you.
There were prayers you whispered because you did not have enough strength to pray loudly.
There were seasons when you could not understand what God was doing.
There were doors that looked permanently closed.
There were losses you thought you would never survive.
There were moments when fear told you, “This is where your story ends.”
Yet somehow…
you are still here.
Maybe wounded.
Maybe rebuilding.
Maybe still carrying questions.
But here.
And the frightening thing about the human heart is that yesterday's miracle can become today's forgotten memory.
Israel knew this pattern.
God provided, and they complained.
God rescued, and they doubted.
God remained faithful, and they wandered.
Before we judge them too quickly, look at us.
How many prayers did we desperately beg God to answer that eventually became blessings we barely notice?
How many things surrounding us today were once things we prayed for?
How quickly can rescue become routine?
How quickly can grace become familiar?
How quickly can a person cry desperately for God in the river and then become spiritually sleepy once standing safely on the shore?
That is why the stones mattered.
Joshua 4:6–7 explains their purpose:
“That this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones? Then ye shall answer them…”
Do not miss that.
God was not merely creating a monument.
He was creating a conversation.
The stones were supposed to make children ask questions.
“Dad…
why are those stones there?”
And suddenly a father would have to remember.
“We didn't put those there because we were strong.”
“We didn't put those there because we defeated the river.”
“We didn't put those there because we figured everything out.”
“Those stones are there because the Jordan stood between us and God's promise…
and God made a way.”
The Hebrew of Joshua 4:7 says the stones would become:
לְזִכָּרוֹן לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַד־עוֹלָם
ləzikkārôn livnê Yiśrāʾēl ʿad-ʿôlām
In context, this means they were to serve as a memorial for the children of Israel enduringly—generation after generation.
A memory with stones attached to it.
Because God did not want His faithfulness buried with the generation that experienced it.
He wanted children who had never stood inside the Jordan to know the God who stopped it.
That should confront every Christian parent.
Every grandfather.
Every grandmother.
Every believer.
Your testimony was never meant to die inside you.
Your children need more than your possessions.
They need to hear what God has done.
They need to know where Jesus found you.
They need to know what He forgave.
They need to know what He restored.
They need to know about the prayers nobody else heard.
They need to know there were moments when you almost surrendered to despair…
but grace kept calling your name.
Tell them.
Tell them about the Jordan.
Tell them about the stones.
But there is something even deeper happening in Joshua 3–4.
The miracle did not begin when Israel became brave enough to conquer the water.
God went before them.
The priests carrying the ark entered first.
Joshua 3:13 says the waters would be cut off when the feet of the priests bearing the ark rested in the Jordan.
The ark represented God's covenant presence among His people.
Israel crossed because God made passage possible.
That distinction matters.
Biblical salvation has always exposed the bankruptcy of human boasting.
We want to tell stories in which we saved ourselves.
“I became stronger.”
“I fixed my life.”
“I found my way.”
“I overcame.”
But the Gospel destroys that illusion.
You did not need a motivational speech.
You needed a Savior.
You did not merely need improvement.
You needed reconciliation with God.
Sin is not simply the collection of unfortunate mistakes we wish we had handled differently.
Sin is rebellion against the holy God who made us.
Scripture says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
The Greek word commonly translated “sin” in that verse is ἥμαρτον — hēmarton, from ἁμαρτάνω (hamartanō).
We have sinned.
All of us.
The respectable.
The religious.
The addicted.
The successful.
The ashamed.
The person reading this with a Bible nearby.
The person reading this while hiding something nobody knows.
All.
That is the scandal.
We cannot carry enough stones, perform enough religious acts, give enough money, attend enough services, or clean ourselves up enough to erase our guilt before God.
But then comes grace.
Romans 3 continues by pointing us toward justification as God's gift through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not the story of bad people becoming impressive.
It is the announcement that sinners can be forgiven and reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Jesus entered the place we could never escape ourselves.
He carried what we could never carry away.
Our guilt.
Our judgment.
Our shame.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And He did not remain in the grave.
Jesus Christ rose.
That is why grace is not positive thinking.
Grace has scars.
Grace has a cross.
Grace has an empty tomb.
Grace has a name.
Jesus.
And perhaps you have spent years carrying stones God never commanded you to carry.
The stone of what you did.
The stone of what they did to you.
The stone of the marriage that collapsed.
The stone of the addiction you keep hiding.
The stone of the secret browser history.
The stone of bitterness.
The stone of hypocrisy.
The stone of the child who walked away.
The stone of the prayer that seems unanswered.
The stone of your past.
You have carried it so long that you started thinking its weight was your identity.
But the twelve stones of Joshua were not monuments to Israel's shame.
They were witnesses to God's faithfulness.
The stone did not say:
“Look how powerful Israel was.”
The stone said:
“Look what God did.”
And that is what Jesus does with surrendered lives.
He does not pretend the past never happened.
He redeems people from it.
Peter's denial remained part of Peter's story.
But denial did not get the final sentence.
Paul's persecution of Christians remained part of Paul's history.
But persecution did not get the final sentence.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet when he turned to Christ, grace reached him even there.
This is why the Gospel is so devastatingly beautiful.
Jesus does not need your edited résumé.
He wants the truth.
The real truth.
The part you crop out before anybody sees it.
The part you bury beneath church language.
The part that still wakes you up sometimes.
Bring that to Christ.
Repentance is not pretending sin does not matter.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who died and rose again.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance, carrying the idea of a changed mind and turning that results in a changed direction.
Grace does not say sin is harmless.
Grace says sin was so serious that Christ went to the cross—and God's love is so astonishing that Christ willingly came for sinners.
Maybe that is why you needed this article today.
Not because you needed another inspirational quote.
Because somewhere along the road, you forgot your stones.
You forgot the hospital room God carried you through.
You forgot the night you begged Jesus for mercy.
You forgot the addiction that once owned you.
You forgot the door God closed that later protected you.
You forgot the people He sent.
You forgot the prayers He answered differently than you expected.
You forgot that there was once a Jordan in front of you…
and somehow God brought you across.
Go back in your memory.
Not to worship the past.
To worship the God who was faithful there.
Because the God of the Jordan was preparing Israel for Jericho.
And sometimes remembering yesterday's faithfulness is how God strengthens His people to face tomorrow's walls.
There is another reason the twelve stones matter.
They represented everybody.
Twelve tribes.
One people.
One testimony.
Nobody could say, “That miracle belongs only to them.”
The memorial belonged to Israel.
And in Christ, something even greater happens.
People who would otherwise have little reason to belong together become one family around one Savior.
Different histories.
Different wounds.
Different languages.
Different nations.
Different failures.
One cross.
One risen Lord.
One Gospel.
That means your testimony may become someone else's stone.
When you say, “Jesus met me there,” somebody drowning in the place you survived realizes the river may not be the end.
When you say, “I had to repent too,” somebody ashamed of their failure realizes Christians are not people who never needed mercy.
When you say, “Christ is still healing me,” somebody who thought healing had to happen instantly realizes sanctification can be a journey of continued dependence on Jesus.
This is why you should not hide every scar.
Some scars become signposts.
Not every detail belongs publicly online, and wisdom still matters.
But never be ashamed of giving Christ glory for what He has redeemed.
Someone in your family may need your testimony.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be silently falling apart.
Someone who looks completely fine may be one night away from abandoning faith.
Someone may have stopped praying.
Someone may think Jesus would never receive someone like them.
And your willingness to share the Gospel may put a stone beside their Jordan.
Send it privately to the believer who has grown tired.
Send it to the person who does not believe yet.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ's saving grace cannot be bought.
We support Gospel work because we have received grace, not because we are trying to purchase it.
But please hear this clearly.
Do not share because you think God will forgive you faster.
Do not buy something because you think generosity purchases salvation.
It does not.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Support should flow from gratitude, worship, stewardship, and a desire to help truth travel farther—not spiritual pressure.
And maybe the most important thing you can do right now costs absolutely nothing.
Be honest.
And if there is something hidden that needs to come into the light before Christ, you do not have to publicly describe your sin.
Let those words become your first small act of honesty.
Then take the deeper step where nobody online can do it for you.
Go to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Ask Him for mercy.
If you already belong to Christ but have wandered, come home.
If your spirit has become cold, ask Him to awaken you.
If shame has kept you hiding, remember the promise of 1 John 1:9: God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
And if you have never truly trusted Christ, understand what the twelve stones ultimately cannot do.
Stones can remind you of a miracle.
They cannot save you.
Religious memories cannot save you.
Christian parents cannot save you.
Church attendance cannot save you.
Only Jesus saves.
The Jordan eventually began flowing again.
The generation that crossed it eventually died.
Even the stones themselves belonged to a world that was passing away.
But Jesus Christ lives.
The One crucified for sinners rose from the dead.
The Gospel does not promise that Christians will never face another river.
It gives us something infinitely greater:
Christ Himself.
So perhaps tonight you need to build a memorial—not necessarily from literal stones, but from remembered grace.
Write down what God has done.
Tell your children.
Tell your spouse.
Call somebody.
Open your Bible.
Remember the prayers.
Remember the rescue.
Remember the correction.
Remember the mercy.
Remember the cross.
And when the enemy points toward everything behind you and whispers,
“Look what you were…”
look toward Jesus and remember what grace has done.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because testimony should have a voice.
Tell us what God brought you through.
Maybe somebody reading your comment is standing exactly where you once stood.
Perhaps that is the hidden beauty of Joshua's stones.
One generation carried them…
so another generation could ask about them.
One generation remembered…
so another could believe that the God who had been faithful before was still worthy of trust.
Your scars do not need to become your throne.
Your shame does not need to become your name.
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your ending.
Jesus does.
And someday, someone may look at the evidence of grace in your life and ask:
“What does this mean?”
May you be able to answer:
“This is where I should have drowned.
This is where I thought everything was over.
This is where I discovered I could not save myself.
And this…
this is where God brought me through.”
Never be ashamed of the stones that remind you where the river should have swallowed you—because they may become the very place where somebody else learns to trust the God who brought you across.
